The Hawai, Chlorodrepanis virens, is a small endemic honeycreeper of the Hawaiian Islands, where its life history traits reflect a long evolutionary history in a relatively stable, predator-free environment. Field studies on the windward slopes of Mauna Loa indicate that newly hatched chicks emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] and possess a remarkably low wet weight at birth of 1.3 grams [Wwb = 1.3 grams]. This neonatal mass is among the smallest recorded for any passerine of comparable adult size, and it underscores the altricial state of the nestlings, which require intensive parental brooding and provisioning. The age at birth is reached after 14 days [ab = 14 days] when eggs are held at the typical nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This relatively short incubation is consistent with the rapid developmental schedule of many island passerines that face minimal nest predation pressure, allowing for a faster turnover of broods within a single breeding season.

Under the typical thermal conditions of the active adult bird, which maintains a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the developmental progression of the Hawai chick follows a predictable trajectory. The time since birth at fledging, defined as the age at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and leaves the nest, is approximately 20 days [tx = approximately 20 days]. at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]At this point, the fledgling, while capable of short flights, remains dependent on its parents for food and guidance during the critical post-fledging period. The maximal lifespan documented for this species under natural conditions is an impressive 12 years [am = 12 years], a longevity that is notably high for a passerine of its body mass and likely reflects the absence of terrestrial mammalian predators in its native cloud forest habitat at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This extended lifespan provides the opportunity for repeated reproductive attempts over many seasons.

The adult body size and the onset of reproductive capability in the Hawai are intimately linked to its foraging ecology, primarily as a nectarivore of ʻōhiʻa lehua and māmane blossoms. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult, representing the maximum recorded body mass in the population, is approximately 12 grams [Wwi = approximately 12 grams]. Young birds attain sexual maturity at a relatively young age, with the time since birth at puberty being approximately 60 days [tp = approximately 60 days] when their body temperature has stabilized at the typical adult value of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early onset of puberty is a common trait among small, short-lived passerines, although the Hawai's subsequent lifespan is considerably extended. The achievement of this developmental stage is marked by the first swelling of the gonads and the initiation of reproductive hormone cascades that prepare the young bird for its first breeding attempt in the following season.

Reproductive output in the Hawai is modest but consistent with its life history strategy as a resident of stable, resource-poor montane forests. Breeding females typically lay 2.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.5 eggs per clutch], a modal clutch size that is common among Hawaiian honeycreepers and suggests a balance between investment per offspring and the energetic costs of parental care. The species is capable of producing multiple broods within a favorable breeding season, and field observations from mid-elevation forests at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] indicate a reproductive frequency of 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = 1.5 clutches per year]. Combining clutch size with the annual number of nesting attempts, the total annual reproductive output averages 3.75 eggs per female. This moderate fecundity is offset by high rates of juvenile survival, enabled by intense biparental care and a relatively long period of post-fledging provisioning that prepares the young for the challenges of independent foraging.

The time elapsed since birth at the first brood, or the age at which a female Hawai successfully rears her first clutch of young, is a full year after hatching, recorded as 365 days [tR = 365 days] when the brooding adult maintains its active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This deferred first reproduction is a direct consequence of the extended period of juvenile provisioning and the need to establish a stable territory with sufficient floral resources to sustain both the parent and her offspring. The delay also reflects the relatively slow pace of life typical of many island endemics. By the time a Hawai reaches its documented maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years], a single individual may have participated in over a dozen breeding seasons at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This repeated reproductive effort, combined with low adult mortality, allows for the gradual accumulation of offspring over a long lifetime, a strategy that is highly adaptive in an unpredictable environment where occasional severe droughts can decimate nectar supplies.
